The words

Great was the day, the joy was great,
When the divine disciples met;
Whilst on their heads the Spirit came,
And sat like tongues of cloven flame.

What gifts, what miracles he gave!
And power to kill, and power to save!
Furnish'd their tongues with wondrous words,
Instead of shields, and spears, and swords.

Thus arm'd, he sent the champions forth
From east to west, from south to north;
"Go, and assert your Saviour's cause,
"Go, spread the mystery of his cross."

These weapons of the holy war,
Of what almighty force they are
To make our stubborn passions bow,
And lay the proudest rebel low!

Nations, the learned and the rude,
Are by these heavenly arms subdu'd;
While Satan rages at his loss,
And hates the doctrine of the cross.

Great King of Grace, my heart subdue,
I would be led in triumph too,
A willing captive to my Lord,
And sing the victories of his word.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum E and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (E), on the word “Great”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Isaac Watts wrote these words for his Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707), Book II, composed on divine subjects, hymn 144, headed “The effusion of the Spirit; or, The success of the gospel”.

Watts' hymns were printed without tunes and sung to any tune of their metre, Long Metre (8.8.8.8). This page sets the words to UXBRIDGE; any other Long Metre tune fits them as well.

  • Words (1707): Isaac Watts (1674–1748)
  • Music (1830): Lowell Mason (1792–1872)

Tune UXBRIDGE by Lowell Mason (1792–1872); words by Isaac Watts (1674–1748).

Sung to the same tune: 'Twas by an Order from the Lord, Behold the Blind Their Sight Receive, Do We Not Know That Solemn Word, Glory to God the Trinity, Had I the Tongues of Greeks and Jews, Here at Thy Cross, My Dying God, High on a Hill of Dazzling Light, In Gabriel's Hand a Mighty Stone, Jesus Is Gone Above the Skies, Life Is the Time to Serve the Lord, Lord, We Are Blind, We Mortals Blind, Man Has a Soul of Vast Desires, No More, My God, I Boast No More, Now Have Our Hearts Embrac'd Our God, Now in the Heat of Youthful Blood, Often I Seek My Lord by Night, Questions and Doubts Be Heard No More, Thus Far the Lord Has Led Me on, Thy Favours Lord, Surprise Our Souls, Up to the Fields Where Angels Lie, Who Can Describe the Joys That Rise.

Questions about Great Was the Day, the Joy Was Great

What is the doh of Great Was the Day, the Joy Was Great?

In this version, in E major, doh is E. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Great Was the Day, the Joy Was Great start on?

It starts on d (E in E major), a pickup on the word “Great” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is Great Was the Day, the Joy Was Great in the public domain?

Yes. Isaac Watts died in 1748, Lowell Mason died in 1872; the words were first published in 1707 and the music in 1830. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
